planting.note: Plant container-grown or own-root stock in spring once frost danger has passed, choosing a sheltered site in colder parts of its range since this Mediterranean species is less cold-hardy than most European wild roses.

directions: Native to rocky scrub and hedgerows around the Mediterranean, this scrambling species rose carries glossy, almost evergreen foliage and bears flat clusters of small single white flowers with a light, musky scent in early summer. It is a once-blooming climber, best trained over a wall, fence, or old tree where its long flexible canes can sprawl and cascade. Give it full sun and well-drained soil, and expect only light, structural pruning after bloom since it flowers on the previous year's growth. It is the wild ancestor of the Sempervirens Group of ramblers bred in early nineteenth-century France.

planting.note: Plant bare-root whips in fall into a hedgerow or informal boundary planting, giving the lax, scrambling canes a hedge, shrub, or low structure to lean against.

directions: A low, trailing-to-scrambling wild rose of western and central European hedgerows and woodland margins, this species produces flat, single white flowers with a boss of golden stamens, opening later in summer than the related dog rose. It roots readily where lax canes touch the ground and tolerates poor, chalky, or shaded soil better than most garden roses, making it valuable for naturalistic hedging and wildlife plantings. Small round red hips follow the flowers and persist into winter, feeding birds. It needs little care beyond occasional thinning of old wood, and is the principal wild parent of the Ayrshire rambling roses.

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root stock in spring with a sturdy pergola, large shrub, or tree in reach, since this vigorous rambler needs substantial support to display its summer flower sprays.

directions: Collected in central China by Ernest Wilson and named for his wife Helen, this rampant once-blooming rambler produces huge trusses of small single white flowers with a strong musky fragrance in midsummer, followed by abundant small orange-red hips. It needs a large tree, wall, or pergola to climb into, as mature plants can cover a substantial structure within a few seasons. Prune only to remove dead or overcrowded canes after flowering, since bloom occurs on growth made the previous year. It is grown chiefly by species-rose collectors and in large gardens that can accommodate its size.

subcategory: species shrub rose grown for hips

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container specimens in early spring, siting the shrub where its fine, arching, almost willow-like growth has room to spread without crowding.

directions: Introduced from western China in the early twentieth century and named for the horticulturist Ellen Willmott, this graceful species rose has fine, ferny, gray-green foliage on slender, gently arching, prickly stems. Small single lilac-pink flowers open in late spring, followed by distinctive small flask-shaped orange-red hips in autumn. It tolerates poor, dry soils once established and needs only occasional removal of old wood to keep the fountain-like form open. It is grown mainly as a specimen or textural foliage shrub by species-rose and collector gardens rather than for a showy flower display.

planting.note: Plant in spring against a warm wall, large tree, or sturdy pergola, giving this vigorous Himalayan climber a sheltered site in regions near the cold edge of its hardiness range.

directions: Native across the Himalayan foothills from Afghanistan to western China, this vigorous once-blooming climber bears large open clusters of musk-scented single white flowers in midsummer, set against soft gray-green foliage. It climbs rampantly by scrambling through trees or over large structures and needs a correspondingly generous support in the garden. It is less cold-tolerant than many Chinese species roses and benefits from a warm, sheltered position in marginal climates. This is the principal wild parent of the climbing rambler 'The Garland' and other musk-scented hybrids.

planting.note: Plant in spring after all frost danger has passed, in a hot, frost-free site with sharp drainage that mimics the arid, rocky slopes of its native Socotra range.

directions: Endemic to the island of Socotra off Yemen, this is the only other species in the pomegranate genus besides the common pomegranate, forming a small drought-adapted tree or large shrub with bright pink-orange flowers. Its fruit is smaller, thinner-walled, and far less palatable than cultivated pomegranate, with pale, less juicy seed pulp, so it is grown chiefly by botanic gardens, pomegranate collectors, and breeders interested in its genetics rather than for eating. It demands full sun, a long hot growing season, and excellent drainage, and has very little cold tolerance, failing outdoors anywhere frost is likely. Interest in the species has grown as a genetic resource for breeding disease resistance and drought tolerance into cultivated pomegranate.
